text:
Moth and Gravel, Field Note 13.
The work outlives the window. An

AI narrated edition of the
published note. An episode is

rendering. You close its window.
What should happen when you open

it again? That question became a
useful test for our podcast

experiment. We already had the
pieces, written field notes,

narration, music, retimed
captions, and a video renderer.

They could produce an episode. A
person still had to remember

which command came next, which
folder held the result, and

which version they had actually
checked. We wanted a small

workbench for that journey.
Somewhere to change the sound,

inspect the consequences, let
the machine work, and come back

with enough context to continue.
A familiar material.

We used Tkinter. The production
engine was already Python, and

an earlier robot workbench had
given us useful experience with

Tk. Themed sections, background
work, and a queue that hands

results back to the interface.
That made it a reasonable

material for this experiment.
The studio could live beside the

existing engine in Ubuntu or WSL
with ordinary desktop controls

and no separate web service to
operate. We kept the production

engine behind an adapter, so
that the interface could change

without taking ownership of
everything underneath it. The

first useful shape was three
stages, produce, review, and

release. Each stage needed a
clear answer to a different

question. What will change? What
have I checked? What is ready to

take to the publisher? Give the
job a life of its own.

The important decision was where
the work should live. The window

holds an editable view. A local
journal keeps drafts, queued

recipes, and job results. A
separate worker owns production.

Closing the window leaves that
worker and its queue in place.

The diagram in the written
edition separates four

responsibilities, with the
window allowed to disappear. It
work was
making

describes the implemented
ownership boundary. Suppose an

episode is queued at 1.15 times
the original pace. Changing the

control afterwards should affect
the next plan. The job already

in the queue keeps the recipe
that was inspected. Unfinished

edits have a different need.
Half a date or an empty numeric

field is perfectly ordinary
while someone is typing. We

preserve that raw text as a
draft and validate it when the

person asks to use it. Returning
to the work should not require

reconstructing a thought that
happened to be incomplete. A

restart can also leave an
uncertain result. In that case,

the journal says interrupted.
There is a saved record to

inspect and an explicit retry.
Guessing that a job succeeded

would make the interface easier
to color green and harder to

trust. Let the labels earn their
confidence. A saved video, a

checked video, and a published
video are different events.

Review therefore belongs to the
saved edition. Listen to it,

check its captions, watch the
full video where appropriate,

and record the confirmations. If
the media changes, the earlier

approval cannot quietly move
across to it. Reopening the

window restores the workspace.
The review checkboxes need

attention again. Release makes
the handoff tangible. It lists

the actual video, thumbnail,
subtitle files, audio, and

transcript with their sizes. A
upload copy comes from the

checked package when one exists.
There is a route to open a file,

a folder, or YouTube Studio, and
a Windows-compatible upload path

when the tool is running in WSL.
Ready for manual upload

describes those local checks.
The person still uploads the

package and records the real
publication details. A local

success message cannot establish
what happened in another

service. A small window exposes
a large assumption. The design

acquired the studio's paper,
ink, and brass, labeled

pictograms, and visible
feedback. The more revealing

it fit. One desktop test run
past while its screenshots

showed an awkward result. The
publishing buttons were visible,

but the editable fields had been
squeezed away at the minimum

window size. The batch checklist
had the same problem. We had

checked that the actions existed
without checking that the

material they acted on remained
usable. We shortened the

guidance, removed competing
folder actions from those

focused panels, and made the
checks cover the fields and

choices themselves. The
screenshot was evidence about a

question the earlier assertions
had missed. A second window

exposes another boundary worth
making explicit. Two copies of

the interface can hold different
drafts of one episode. A newer

checkpoint needs an identity,
and the other window needs a

chance to resolve that conflict
while keeping its edits. Saved

should mean that this version
was saved, enough to use with a
next question.

By the end of the first complete
pass, the studio had durable

drafts, sound controls, editable
publishing copy, batch

inspection, and worker health.
Its verification included 86

tests with 31 exercising real Tk
controls. A separate production

run finished all 13 existing
recordings, checked their

retimed captions, and rendered
short video previews and

thumbnails. A repeat run checked
cache reuse. Those are useful

boundaries for the result. They
establish considerably more than

a promising mock-up. They do not
replace listening to the

finished episodes or completing
the browser upload. The next

question is close at hand. Can
this workbench help us release

its own field note without
someone keeping the terminal

sequence in their head? There is
still a gap at the beginning.

Studio starts from prepared
recordings. A new written note

needs a narration script, a
deliberate generation step, and

captions before it reaches that
shelf. That handoff deserves the

same care as the final upload,
visible prerequisites, an

inspectable plan, and a clear
account of any service being

used. For now, the experiment
has become a usable local tool

for the episodes we already
have. The next specimen is this

note. Experiment record, working
software. What this pass

establishes. The first pass
counts and desktop capture refer

to the implementation linked in
the written edition. Its native

desktop checks and real media
production run passed. The

capture is a controlled fixture,
and the ownership graphic is a

schematic. The production run
rendered short previews rather

than full-length videos of the
entire collection. The

continuing implementation and
studio guide contain the current

behavior and validation. Native
Windows packaging, embedded

playback, and authenticated
publishing remain outside this

local Linux/WSL experiment.
Narration and publication of

this note are separate steps
from the verification described

here. You have been listening to
Moth and Gravel Field Notes. The

written edition is at
mothandgravel.com.
